findings.title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute for all jobs
findings.body: The ticker in CleanUpService.Run is changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, but this ticker drives srv.clean(), which runs every cleanup job (expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, and query history), not just annotation cleanup. This increases the frequency and database/filesystem load of all of those jobs tenfold without any justification in the PR description and can worsen the MySQL contention the PR is trying to reduce.

findings.title: Normal cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists
findings.body: CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags call r.log.Error for every batch (including successful batches, an empty final batch, and cases where the logged err is nil at line 534). Routine successful cleanup will therefore generate error-level log noise/alerts, and including the entire ids slice (potentially tens of thousands of IDs with a large batch size) makes each message very large. These should be Debug/Info-level summaries without dumping all IDs.

findings.title: Split fetch/delete can over-delete annotations kept by the MaxCount rule
findings.body: For MaxCount cleanup, fetchIDs selects IDs using LIMIT batch OFFSET MaxCount at one instant, then deleteByIDs deletes those IDs in a separate statement/session without rechecking that they are still beyond MaxCount. If annotations that were within the newest MaxCount are deleted concurrently between the fetch and the delete, some fetched annotations may no longer be excess and should now be retained, but they will still be deleted. The previous single DELETE evaluated the excess condition atomically in one statement.

findings.title: Placeholder-limit workaround only handles SQLite
findings.body: deleteByIDs builds one '?' placeholder per ID for every non-SQLite database, bounded only by AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize. The new large-batch test uses a batch size of 32767; on databases with prepared-statement placeholder limits (notably PostgreSQL's 65535 limit is only about twice that, and deployments can configure an even larger batch size), a sufficiently large configured batch will now fail with a parameter-limit error, whereas the previous subquery DELETE did not pass IDs as parameters at all. The check also uses the configured batch size rather than len(ids). Either inline IDs or chunk deletes based on the actual ID count for all dialects with limits.
